title: Gaulton T1D Effector Genes method
bodyHtml:
This prioritization of putative ‘effector’ genes causal for disease risk at known type 1 diabetes (T1D) loci was performed by Kyle Gaulton, University of California at San Diego.  The criteria used in prioritizing genes included (i) fine-mapped T1D coding variants in the gene, (ii) relevant phenotype when the gene is perturbed in an animal or human cell model system, and (iii) fine-mapped T1D non-coding variants with regulatory links to the gene.

Sections:

I. Definition of T1D loci and genes at T1D loci
II. Coding variant genetic evidence
III. Model system evidence
IV. Epigenomic evidence
V. QTL evidence
VI. Prioritizing genes
VII. Plans for future versions

I. Definition of T1D loci and genes at T1D loci

We identified 92 total loci that reached genome-wide significance (p-value < 5x10-8) in Chiou et al. 2021, Barrett et al. 2009, Bradfield et al. 2011, Onengut-Gumuscu et al. 2015, or Cooper et al. 2008. At each locus, we defined the genomic region of interest as 1MB in either direction of the variant with the highest causal probability (PPA) in fine-mapping data from Chiou et al. 2021. At loci with multiple independent signals, we took the union of genomic regions of interest across signals. For the MHC locus, we defined the genomic region of interest as 28.50Mb to 33.50Mb (hg19) on chromosome 6.

We then identified all genes in GENCODE v36 where a transcription start site (TSS) of a protein-coding transcript of the gene mapped within the genomic region of interest for any locus. This resulted in a list of 1,408 unique genes which were considered in "effector" gene prioritization.

II. Coding variant genetic evidence

First, we identified all genes with a protein-altering (missense, nonsense, frameshift) variant in fine-mapping credible sets (probability of .10 or greater) in Chiou et al. 2021 or Onengut-Gumuscu et al. 2015.

Second, we identified all genes that cause a monogenic form of diabetes or autoimmune disease in the OMIM database.

Third, we identified class I, class II or class III MHC genes with haplotypes affecting T1D risk reported in Noble et al. 2000, Noble and Erlich 2012, Noble and Valdes 2011, Alizadeh et al. 2017, Noble et al. 2010.

III. Model system evidence

We collected evidence for genes affecting T1D, or a cellular phenotype relevant to T1D, in mouse models and human cell models.

First, we used the Mouse Genome Database (MGD) to identify genes reported to produce one of the following phenotypes when perturbed in a mouse model: increased susceptibility to autoimmune diabetes (MP:0004803) or decreased susceptibility to autoimmune diabetes (MP:0004804).

Second, we identified genes affecting beta cell survival in a CRISPR loss of function screen in NIT-1 cells transplanted into NOD mice (Cai et al. 2020).

Third, we identified genes with genetic differences affecting susceptibility to T1D in NOD mice (Dooley et al. 2016).

Fourth, we identified genes which affected cell survival using siRNA, shRNA or over-expression in beta cell models in response to disease-relevant stimuli (across multiple publications, listed in the table with the evidence for each gene).

IV. Epigenomic evidence

We collected evidence for genes linked to T1D risk variants using epigenomic data such as 3D chromatin interactions, activity-by-contact (ABC) predictions and single cell co-accessibility.

First, we identified variants in fine-mapping credible sets with PPA>.10 from Chiou et al. 2021 in candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) that had ABC links to a gene promoter in all T lymphocyte, monocyte, and pancreatic cell types included in the study. We excluded cCREs that had ABC predicted links to more than five genes in a cell type.

Second, we identified variants in fine-mapping credible sets with PPA>.10 from Chiou et al. 2021 in cCREs that had single cell co-accessibility with a gene promoter in T lymphocyte, monocyte, and pancreatic cell types included in the study. We excluded cCREs that had ABC predicted links to more than five genes in a cell type.

Third, we identified variants in fine-mapping credible sets with PPA>.10 from Chiou et al. 2021 overlapping cCREs in unstimulated and stimulated T cell populations from Calderon et al. 2019. We then defined cCREs linked to gene promoters using promoter capture Hi-C data in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from Javierre et al. 2016. We excluded cCREs that had ABC predicted links to more than five genes in a cell type.

V. QTL evidence

We collected evidence for genes linked to T1D risk variants using molecular QTLs.

First, we identified genes with significant eQTLs to fine-mapped T1D variants with PPA>.10 in Chiou et al. 2021 from the eQTL catalogue using the following studies: Alasoo et al. 2018 (macrophages); BLUEPRINT (monocytes, neutrophils, CD4+ T lymphocytes); GenCord (LCLs, T cells); GEUVADIS (LCLs); Schmiedel et al. 2018 (15 immune cell types); TwinsUK (LCLs, blood); CAP (LCLs); Nédélec et al. 2016 (macrophages); Lepik et al. 2017 (blood); van de Bunt et al. 2015 (islets).

Second, we identified eQTLs colocalized with T1D risk signals from Wallace et al. 2012.

Third, we identified genes or proteins with reported significant QTLs at T1D loci across multiple different studies of specific loci.

VI. Prioritizing genes

In total, 178 genes representing 65 T1D loci had at least one line of evidence for being an 'effector' gene. We prioritized genes by grouping them into five 'tiers' based on this evidence.

  • Tier 1: Genes that are causal or almost certainly causal for disease based on genetics, with a protein-altering variant causal for T1D or a relevant monogenic disease
  • Tier 2: Genes with strong evidence based on both genetics and biology, with (i) phenotype in a relevant animal or cell perturbation model and (ii) epigenome and/or QTL link to T1D variant
  • Tier 3: Genes with strong evidence based on biology only, with a phenotype in a relevant animal or cell perturbation model
  • Tier 4: Genes with strong evidence based on genetics only, with an epigenome and QTL link to T1D variant
  • Tier 5: Genes with lower evidence based on genetics, based on only one of epigenome link to T1D variant or QTL to T1D variant

VII. Plans for future versions

Incorporate additional genetic T1D loci and fine-mapping data, including data from Robertson et al. 2021, and any other genetic studies of T1D which are published.

Incorporate colocalization tests of eQTL catalog data to identify eQTLs shared with T1D risk signals at each locus, as opposed to just using T1D variants with significant eQTLs.
